source_document.body:
Packaged goods supply chains are full of examples of exception requests, like when a retailer asks for a custom pack configuration, a key account needs a special label, or a shipment gets rerouted on short notice to hit a delivery window. Those kinds of exceptions aren’t necessarily problems on their own. Exception handling can look like good customer service. But on Oct. 15, FreightWaves and G3 Logistics are asking what happens when you stop counting those requests one at a time and start adding them up.
That’s the topic of The Hidden Cost-to-Serve in Packaged Goods: Managing Rework, Specialized Handling, and Operational Exceptions , a free webinar that will dig into the repack jobs, relabeling work, retailer-specific requirements, and expedited changes that accumulate inside packaged goods networks until they’re no longer exceptions at all. Without visibility into what those exceptions cost, they can be devastating to margins over time.
G3 Logistics brings transportation, warehousing, and supply chain expertise to a common packaged goods challenge: customer requests that add work beyond the standard flow. A package change, relabeling request, or tighter delivery window can affect handling, schedules, inventory, and capacity across multiple teams. Seeing those effects together helps leaders understand hidden costs and make more intentional service decisions.
Jerry Knight, G3’s Senior Director of Global Logistics, and Nicole Ostertag, Head of Solutions, will explore when a reasonable exception becomes a recurring operating cost—and what should change when it does.
A one-off retailer packaging request for a promotion can look like a manageable commercial accommodation, until the extra handling, line interruptions, inventory segregation, and tighter turnaround windows it requires start showing up in every subsequent run for that account. Rework that begins as occasional recovery work (such as relabeling, repacking, or fixing damaged product) can quietly become a standing part of daily operations, its cost buried inside standard labor instead of tracked anywhere finance or ops can see it. The accounts that matter most commercially are often the ones creating the most operational drag, including frequent small runs, narrow delivery windows, or constant manual workarounds to hit a service level that is now taken for granted.
The discussion is structured as a working session for supply chain leaders to compare notes on where these costs show up first, which ones are easy to see on a P&L, which stay buried in additional touches and lost throughput, and who in the organization actually owns the decision to say yes to a request. The webinar is designed to give you a sharper read on how to measure hidden costs at the customer, SKU or channel level, where other companies have had success clawing back margin through order rules, packaging redesign, customer segmentation or clearer exception pricing, and a clearer sense of which functions need to be in the same room to make any of it stick.
Hidden costs rarely announce themselves as a logistics problem or a warehouse problem. They sit at the intersection of commercial commitments, packaging decisions, and operational execution. Leaders can address them by making exceptions visible before workarounds become part of daily operations.
The webinar is free to attend. If you’re responsible for packaging, operations, planning, or customer service in a packaged goods supply chain, you’ll want to be in the room before the hidden costs in your own network get any harder to see.
